title: Get out, Mara
hookLine: Moggallana feels Mara in his belly and tells him to come out

cards: A heaviness in the stomach can arrive for no clear reason. Dread before a meeting. A sourness after a phone call.

It's easy to carry it around all afternoon without ever asking what it is. One day the monk Moggallana was walking up and down in the open air, practicing, and his belly suddenly felt heavy, as if it were full of beans.
He stopped. He went inside, sat down, and looked.

teach.h: MARA: A TEMPTER, OR A FORCE IN THE MIND
teach.b: This is the fiftieth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the rebuke to Mara.
Mara is the tempter of the Buddhist stories: the voice of distraction, fear and craving, sometimes told as a being, sometimes heard as a force in the mind. Yesterday he hid in a god's assembly.
Here, the text says, he had slipped into Moggallana's belly.

Moggallana turns his attention inward, sees him, and speaks plainly: come out, Evil One. Come out. Don't trouble the Buddha or the Buddha's disciple, or it will bring you harm and suffering for a long time.
Mara thinks: he doesn't really know me. Even his teacher wouldn't recognize me that fast. Moggallana answers the thought: I know you.
Don't think I don't. So Mara comes out of his mouth and stands leaning against the door bar.
I see you there too, says Moggallana. Then he tells an old story. Long ago, he says, I was a Mara myself, named Dusi, and you were my sister's son, my nephew.
He tells what happened when that Mara tormented a Buddha of an earlier age, and how it ended badly for him. Mara, the text says, is dismayed, and disappears.
Look at how the scene works.
Moggallana doesn't fight, or panic, or pretend the heaviness isn't there. He stops, sits, looks, and names it. I see you.
And what is seen clearly often loosens its grip. Some meditation teachers call this naming: seeing a mood clearly and calling it what it is, without fighting it.

how: In several early Buddhist stories, Mara leaves once he is recognized ('I know you, Mara'); some meditation teachers use this as a model for noting or naming difficult mind-states without suppressing them.

o: a curse that drives away bad luck
Moggallana's words telling Mara to leave
a monk's rule for unwanted guests

games.q: the story of the heavy belly — tap the pairs.
p: heavy, as if full of beans
even his teacher couldn't spot me that fast
where Mara stands after coming out
a Mara long ago, Moggallana himself

s: Moggallana fought Mara with his powers
he simply sat, looked, saw him, and said: come out. I see you.
Moggallana says he himself was once a Mara named Dusi
he tells Mara that long ago he was Dusi, and Mara was his sister's son.
Mara left the moment Moggallana felt the heaviness
the heaviness came first; Mara left only after Moggallana stopped, looked and named him.

games.q: you're walking in meditation and your belly suddenly feels heavy, as if full of beans. what does Moggallana do?
o: walk faster to shake it off.
go inside, sit down, and look at it.
ignore it and finish the walk.
games.why: he goes in, sits, turns attention inward, and sees Mara there. seen clearly, Mara comes out.

practice: Scan the body slowly, the jaw, the shoulders, the chest, the belly, and if you find a weight, a tightness or a flutter, stop there and ask quietly: what are you?
Worry, irritation, sadness: let a name come, and say inwardly, I see you. Don't push it out; let it stand by the door, seen, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Get out. The heart of Moggallana's plain words to Mara, come out, spoken only after he had stopped, looked, and seen him clearly.

orig.note: Pali Mara: the tempter, called the Evil One in this discourse.

carryVoice: Your line: I see you. Moggallana's whole answer was a clear look. Day four hundred forty-two.
